item.title: How Wall Street Is Bracing For the Post-Jensen Huang Nvidia Era
item.ns0:encoded:
Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era has just begun and there are so many open questions about the company's future. Who will the board choose to be Nvidia's next CEO? Will the government crack down on the chipmaker's business practices, particularly in Asia? And will Nvidia's uncertain position begin to spillover into the wider AI ecosystem, from the labs to data center providers? Stacy Rasgon, managing director and senior analyst at Bernstein, isn't optimistic about the short term future of Nvidia and he talks to us today about the cloudy outlook at the company in the wake of Jensen's resignation. We also discuss why he chose to downgrade Nvidia's stock, the surreal experience of covering Jensen's fall as an analyst, and what he's paying attention to ahead of Nvidia's earnings.

item.title: Why a $2 Billion Law Firm Suddenly Collapsed
item.ns0:encoded:
At the end of October, seemingly overnight, a major law firm called Weil Gotshal announced it was winding down after a number of partners departed and talks of a merger with another firm failed. So how did a $2 billion big law firm collapse in the span of a few weeks? In 2015, Yale Law professor John Morley published a paper called "Why Law Firms Collapse," that now looks very prescient, with his idea of a “partner run," or the law firm version of a bank run. What is especially interesting about Morley's paper is his forensic examination of partner-led businesses and the idea that the model might be inherently fragile. In this episode, we talk to Morley about his newly relevant paper, the collapse of Weil Gotshal, whether AI will really change how law firms are run, and the future of big law.

Read more:

item.title: What Nvidia's Megaspeed Scandal Is Really All About
item.ns0:encoded:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, whom US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, is one of the biggest stories in the world right now. Bloomberg News tech reporter Mackenzie Hawkins has been paying close attention to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based neocloud that Alice Huang was a former executive at — and one of Nvidia’s largest buyers of chips in Southeast Asia. Hawkins is an expert when it comes to the geopolitics of chips, and she tells us that the story that blew up in the last week has been brewing for a while. The US government was investigating suspected chip diversion involving Megaspeed as early as last year. (Megaspeed denies wrongdoing and Nvidia says it found no evidence of chip smuggling.) On this episode, we talk to Hawkins about how she and our Bloomberg News colleagues began investigating Megaspeed and its relationship to Nvidia, the raging debate in Washington over chip export controls, and the incredibly sophisticated and opaque mechanics of chip smuggling itself.

item.title: The Perfect Storm That Clobbered Hedge Funds
item.ns0:encoded:
Even before the US midterms, the AI trade was weakening. Just look at all the headlines from October in the hedge fund world — it was one of the bloodiest periods the industry has faced in recent memory. Now, after the blue wave, things continue to look uncertain. So what's going to happen with the AI buildout now? And what about the big Anthropic IPO? Today's episode is a two-parter, one that examines both the hedge fund carnage of the last few weeks and the broader macro conditions we find ourselves in after the midterm elections. We speak with two of our Bloomberg News colleagues — Nishant Kumar, chief correspondent for hedge funds, and macro strategist Michael Ball — and they help lay out why October was a historic month for hedge funds and what they are paying attention to now as jitters from the AI trade continue to work their way through the market.

Read more: Crowded Hedge Fund Trades Unwind Fast After Ugly October

item.title: This Is How New York City Takes Out Its Trash
item.ns0:encoded:
According to Joshua Goodman, trash collection in New York is one of the last services the city offers that is not yet touched by neoliberalism. What he means is that it's the last free and unlimited city service — there is no opt-in; it is not means tested. Goodman — who is the DSNY's deputy commissioner for public affairs and customer experience — tells us that the city deals with 24 million pounds of trash every day, and on today's podcast, he explains the logistical dance required to sort through all that garbage. We also get into why NYC produces less trash than you might think, the DSNY's new containerization program (and the new side-loading trucks they built in less than 18 months), and why recycling is not a scam.
